content.content:
# Issue tracker: GitHub

Issues and specs for this repo live as GitHub issues. Use the `gh` CLI for all operations.

## Conventions

- **Create an issue**: `gh issue create --title "..." --body "..."`. Use a heredoc for multi-line bodies.
- **Read an issue**: `gh issue view <number> --json number,title,body,labels,comments`.
- **List issues**: `gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments --jq '[.[] | {number, title, body, labels: [.labels[].name], comments: [.comments[].body]}]'` with appropriate `--label` and `--state` filters.
- **Make an issue a sub-issue of a parent**: `gh issue create --parent <parent> ...`, or `gh issue edit <parent> --add-sub-issue <child>` afterwards (`gh` 2.94+). Older `gh`: `gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<parent>/sub_issues -F sub_issue_id=<child-db-id>` (database id, as in **Blocking** below). Without sub-issues, put `Part of #<parent>` at the top of the child body.
- **Blocking**: GitHub's **native issue dependencies**, the canonical, UI-visible representation. Add an edge with `gh issue create --blocked-by <n>,<n> ...` or `gh issue edit <child> --add-blocked-by <blocker>` (`gh` 2.94+). Older `gh`: `gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<child>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=<blocker-db-id>`, where `<blocker-db-id>` is the blocker's numeric **database id** (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .id`, _not_ the `#number` or `node_id`). Where dependencies aren't available, fall back to a `Blocked by: #<n>, #<n>` line at the top of the child body. A ticket is unblocked when every blocker is closed.
- **Count open blockers**: `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by` (open blockers only; 0 means startable). `gh issue view <n> --json blockedBy` also lists closed blockers, so filter it: `--jq '[.blockedBy.nodes[] | select(.state == "OPEN")] | length'`.
- **Comment on an issue**: `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`
- **Apply / remove labels**: `gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..."` / `--remove-label "..."`
- **Close**: post the explanation with `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`, then `gh issue close <number>`. On an already-closed issue, `gh issue close --comment` drops the comment and still exits 0.

Infer the repo from `git remote -v`; `gh` does this automatically when run inside a clone.

File issues only into the user's own repo. Never file into `mattpocock/skills` (the repo these skills come from) unless the user owns it. In a fork, `gh` can default to the upstream parent, so before the first `gh issue create` of a session, check the target with `gh repo view --json nameWithOwner` and confirm it with the user if it is not their repo.

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.** _(Set to `yes` if this repo treats external PRs as feature requests; `/triage` reads this flag.)_

When set to `yes`, PRs run through the same labels and states as issues, using the `gh pr` equivalents:

- **Read a PR**: `gh pr view <number>`, then `gh pr view <number> --comments` (off a TTY, `--comments` prints only the comments, not the body), and `gh pr diff <number>` for the diff.
- **List external PRs for triage**: `gh api --paginate 'repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls?state=open' --jq '.[] | select(.author_association | IN("OWNER","MEMBER","COLLABORATOR") | not) | {number, title, author: .user.login, author_association, labels: [.labels[].name]}'`.
- **Comment / label / close**: `gh pr comment`, `gh pr edit --add-label`/`--remove-label`, `gh pr close`.

GitHub shares one number space across issues and PRs, so a bare `#42` may be either: resolve with `gh pr view 42` and fall back to `gh issue view 42`.

## When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"

Create a GitHub issue.

## When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"

Read it as in **Read an issue** above.

## Wayfinding operations

Used by `/wayfinder`. The **map** is a single issue with **child** issues as tickets.

- **Map**: a single issue labelled `wayfinder:map`, holding the Notes / Decisions-so-far / Fog body. `gh issue create --label wayfinder:map`.
- **Child ticket**: an issue linked to the map as a GitHub sub-issue (see **Make an issue a sub-issue of a parent**). Where sub-issues aren't enabled, add the child to a task list in the map body and put `Part of #<map>` at the top of the child body. Labels: `wayfinder:<type>` (`research`/`prototype`/`grilling`/`task`). Once claimed, the ticket is assigned to the driving dev.
- **Blocking**: see **Blocking** under Conventions.
- **Frontier query**: list the map's open children (`gh issue list --state open`, scoped to the map's sub-issues / task list), drop any with an open blocker (see **Count open blockers**, or an open issue in the `Blocked by` line) or an assignee; first in map order wins.
- **Claim**: `gh issue edit <n> --add-assignee @me`, the session's first write.
- **Resolve**: `gh issue comment <n> --body "<answer>"`, then `gh issue close <n>`, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far.

content.content:
=================== #239
Remove the Worker-side EmailOutbox: the Organization object now queues every send it creates
Follow-up to #238.

The fix for #238 adds a transactional outbox to the Organization Durable Object: every send it creates or requeues is put on the Email queue by its alarm. The Worker-side `EmailOutbox` (domain `DirectoryFlow`, `PulseFlow`; `MainWorker` wiring; `queueEmail` in `EmailTestRoutes`) still queues the same sends, so those get two queue messages. `deliver` claims each send once, so this is harmless but leaves two dispatchers.

Remove `EmailOutbox` and its callers and test fakes, and rely on the object's outbox alone.
SUB: 
COMMENTS:
Also in scope: make `TestInvitationTestRoutes` independent of automatic delivery. It claims and settles a test send by hand (`claimEmailSend(failing, …)`), which can race the Organization outbox delivering that send first (raised on #240). Options: a reject mode in `CapturingEmailSender` for a marked recipient, or one fixture RPC that creates and fails a send in one transaction.

=================== #232
Signed-in production pass: copy, plural and Round-label fixes
Part of #137. Found on 2026-11-17 on production, signed in with an email code (desktop, English, light). Everything else on the Teams list, Team page checklist, Pulse editor, Settings and My history rendered as designed with no horizontal overflow.

- [ ] **Sign-in copy promises Google and Microsoft.** The sign-in card says "Use a code sent to your email, or your Google or Microsoft account." The page has no such buttons (ADR 0022 only keeps them if Better Auth can configure them inside the Worker). Drop the clause until they exist.
- [ ] **Code expiry disagrees.** After requesting a code the page says "It expires in 5 minutes." The email says "It expires in 10 minutes." Make one number.
- [ ] **"1 people".** The Pulse editor says "This Team has 1 people, fewer than the 4 needed…". Use the `.one`/`.other` plural pair, in the German catalog too.
- [ ] **Round title and window disagree.** The Rounds list titles a Round "Round Nov 24, 2026" while its window reads "Nov 18, 2026 to Nov 19, 2026"; an open Round titled "Round Nov 23, 2026" read "Nov 17 to Nov 24". After a Pulse's day or time changes, the title keeps the date of the Round as first planned. Title it from the window's open date.
- [ ] **A Round with nobody to invite says nothing.** A Team whose only Person is its Lead opens a Round and sends no Invitation, and nothing on the Rounds screen, the Team page or Failed emails says so (SPEC §7: no invitation skipped silently). Likewise a Member added after a Round opens gets the "added" email but no Invitation until the next Round, with no hint. Say who was invited, and who was not and why.
- [ ] **Signed-out console noise.** `GET /auth/session` answers 401 on every signed-out load, which Chrome logs as a console error. Answer 200 with a signed-out body, or leave it.
- [ ] **Answer page error box.** Tracked in #231 (it is also unstyled).

Not covered yet: German, dark mode, phone width, and a real Round's Invitation, Results and Actions (the first real Round opens 2026-11-18 06:00 Berlin on the "Claude Test" Team).
SUB: 
COMMENTS:
Fixed in #235: sign-in intro, code lifetime (one number, now `Policy.signIn.codeMinutes` via #237), '1 person', Round title from the window's open date (Rounds list, home, Team checklist).

Still open: a Round with nobody to invite says nothing (needs a decision on where to show it); signed-out `/auth/session` 401 (API contract change); Results/history/overview still title from `plannedOpenDate`. German is out of scope now (#236, ADR 0025).

=================== #230
CI: spend the preview stage only on the revisions that need it
The preview workflow is the largest single cost in CI, and the run decides most of its work only after it has already started. A stage is deployed for every push, then smoke-tested, privacy-read-back, and driven by the end-to-end suite, even when the pull request has already moved on or when the diff cannot change a deployed byte.

## Measured baseline

`node scripts/ci/runner-minutes.mjs --days 7`, over 7 days to 2026-11-17:

| Workflow | Runs | Runner minutes | Per job |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CI | 153 | 312 | check 1.6m, privacy 0.4m |
| Preview | 118 | 363 | deploy 1.2m, e2e 1.9m, preview-privacy 1.7m, destroy 0.7m |
| Deploy | 60 | 243 | staging deploy 0.8m, staging-e2e 1.0m, staging-privacy 1.9m, production 0.9m |
| **All** | | **918 (131 per day, about $31 per 30 days at $0.008/minute)** | |

A pull request's required answer arrives in about 90 s. The preview stage adds about 4.8 runner-minutes and about five minutes of wall time per revision. These are GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runners, so the money at stake is small; feedback time and not starting work nobody needs are the point.

## What the article's numbers do not transfer

The OpenClaw post reports 86.5% fewer runner-hours on sponsored runners over a 4M-line test suite. Here the whole suite is 82 test files and finishes in 18 s locally (62 s on a runner). Sharding, dependency-based test selection and a test-line budget would each cost more than they save at this size. What transfers is the ordering: decide before you pay for setup, and make the decision inspectable and tested.

Backtested against this repository's own history, before choosing: the superseded-revision guard would have skipped 2 of the last 100 preview runs (1.3 runner-minutes) — it pays when three or more pushes land inside one run's ~4.5 minutes, which is an agent loop rather than today's cadence. The prose-only gate covers 2 of those 100 runs (8.9 runner-minutes, ~4% of preview compute) and 7 of the last 100 pull requests, because documentation work is a real share of this repo's changes.

## Steps

- [ ] **1. Measure before changing anything.** `scripts/ci/runner-minutes.mjs` reads the Actions API and prints runner minutes per workflow and per job, with an estimated cost at a configurable price. Re-run it after each step.
- [ ] **2. Move the preview path rules out of YAML.** `scripts/ci/select.mjs` classifies a changed-path list, with `select.test.ts` beside it. The two rules that already exist (the Submission-path canary, the answer-entry Lighthouse gate) move verbatim and are locked by tests; verified against 40 real commits with no behaviour change. `preview.yml` then reads the classification once per run instead of running two inline `grep`s in three jobs.
- [ ] **3. Stop a superseded revision before it pays for a stage.** One `gh api pulls/<n>` read as the first step of the `deploy` job, before checkout or install. A revision that is no longer the head stops in about ten seconds and leaves the stage to the newer run. A failed API read deploys: being unsure is a reason to run the check.
- [ ] **4. Skip the stage when the diff cannot reach it.** Prose (`docs/`, any `*.md`), agent instructions, hooks and `scripts/` get no stage; a mixed or empty diff always deploys. `preview-privacy` and `e2e` skip with it, and the Lighthouse build no longer runs when its gate is not required.
- [ ] **5. Record the decision.** ADR 0025 (the gates, the rejected options and the backtest) and the preview section of `docs/infra.md`.
- [ ] **6. Re-measure and record the result here.** `node scripts/ci/runner-minutes.mjs --days 7` after a week of the new workflow, posted as a comment on this issue, with feedback time read beside compute cost.

## Done when

- A prose-only pull request reaches its answer without deploying a stage, and the privacy job, the canary sweep and the Lighthouse gate still run wherever they are required.
- A push that supersedes a queued revision leaves that revision with a ten-second `deploy` job instead of a full stage.
- `ci.yml` is unchanged: typecheck, the ledgers, formatting, lint, the web build, the unit suite with coverage and the separate privacy job run on every pull request and every push to `main`.
- `deploy.yml` is unchanged: staging and production deploy after every successful `main` run, and the staging canary sweep still runs every time.
- `pnpm test scripts/ci/select.test.ts` fails if a path rule changes without being meant.
- The re-measurement in step 6 is posted here.

## Not in this issue

- **Gating the Deploy workflow by changed paths.** A `workflow_run` payload does not say how many commits a push carried, so the tip's diff can miss a Submission-path change earlier in the same push, and a privacy invariant is a release blocker (SPEC §7). Revisit only with a reliable push range, for example by diffing against the last deployed SHA.
- **`cancel-in-progress: true` on the preview group.** It interrupts a half-applied Alchemy deploy or destroy; the revision guard removes the same waste without interrupting anything.
- **Workflow-level `paths:` filters.** A filtered run reports no check at all, so a reviewer cannot tell "not needed" from "not reported".
- **Caching Playwright browsers in the `e2e` job.** Worth about 30 s per run; measure it before adding a cache key.
- **Splitting the `check` job.** The suite is the dominant step (62 s) and runs in parallel with nothing today; splitting would buy ~25 s of wall time and pay a second setup.

## Status

=================== #230
CI: spend the preview stage only on the revisions that need it
The preview workflow is the largest single cost in CI, and the run decides most of its work only after it has already started. A stage is deployed for every push, then smoke-tested, privacy-read-back, and driven by the end-to-end suite, even when the pull request has already moved on or when the diff cannot change a deployed byte.

## Measured baseline

`node scripts/ci/runner-minutes.mjs --days 7`, over 7 days to 2026-11-17:

| Workflow | Runs | Runner minutes | Per job |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CI | 153 | 312 | check 1.6m, privacy 0.4m |
| Preview | 118 | 363 | deploy 1.2m, e2e 1.9m, preview-privacy 1.7m, destroy 0.7m |
| Deploy | 60 | 243 | staging deploy 0.8m, staging-e2e 1.0m, staging-privacy 1.9m, production 0.9m |
| **All** | | **918 (131 per day, about $31 per 30 days at $0.008/minute)** | |

A pull request's required answer arrives in about 90 s. The preview stage adds about 4.8 runner-minutes and about five minutes of wall time per revision. These are GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runners, so the money at stake is small; feedback time and not starting work nobody needs are the point.

## What the article's numbers do not transfer

The OpenClaw post reports 86.5% fewer runner-hours on sponsored runners over a 4M-line test suite. Here the whole suite is 82 test files and finishes in 18 s locally (62 s on a runner). Sharding, dependency-based test selection and a test-line budget would each cost more than they save at this size. What transfers is the ordering: decide before you pay for setup, and make the decision inspectable and tested.

Backtested against this repository's own history, before choosing: the superseded-revision guard would have skipped 2 of the last 100 preview runs (1.3 runner-minutes) — it pays when three or more pushes land inside one run's ~4.5 minutes, which is an agent loop rather than today's cadence. The prose-only gate covers 2 of those 100 runs (8.9 runner-minutes, ~4% of preview compute) and 7 of the last 100 pull requests, because documentation work is a real share of this repo's changes.

## Steps

- [ ] **1. Measure before changing anything.** `scripts/ci/runner-minutes.mjs` reads the Actions API and prints runner minutes per workflow and per job, with an estimated cost at a configurable price. Re-run it after each step.
- [ ] **2. Move the preview path rules out of YAML.** `scripts/ci/select.mjs` classifies a changed-path list, with `select.test.ts` beside it. The two rules that already exist (the Submission-path canary, the answer-entry Lighthouse gate) move verbatim and are locked by tests; verified against 40 real commits with no behaviour change. `preview.yml` then reads the classification once per run instead of running two inline `grep`s in three jobs.
- [ ] **3. Stop a superseded revision before it pays for a stage.** One `gh api pulls/<n>` read as the first step of the `deploy` job, before checkout or install. A revision that is no longer the head stops in about ten seconds and leaves the stage to the newer run. A failed API read deploys: being unsure is a reason to run the check.
- [ ] **4. Skip the stage when the diff cannot reach it.** Prose (`docs/`, any `*.md`), agent instructions, hooks and `scripts/` get no stage; a mixed or empty diff always deploys. `preview-privacy` and `e2e` skip with it, and the Lighthouse build no longer runs when its gate is not required.
- [ ] **5. Record the decision.** ADR 0025 (the gates, the rejected options and the backtest) and the preview section of `docs/infra.md`.
- [ ] **6. Re-measure and record the result here.** `node scripts/ci/runner-minutes.mjs --days 7` after a week of the new workflow, posted as a comment on this issue, with feedback time read beside compute cost.

## Done when

- A prose-only pull request reaches its answer without deploying a stage, and the privacy job, the canary sweep and the Lighthouse gate still run wherever they are required.
- A push that supersedes a queued revision leaves that revision with a ten-second `deploy` job instead of a full stage.
- `ci.yml` is unchanged: typecheck, the ledgers, formatting, lint, the web build, the unit suite with coverage and the separate privacy job run on every pull request and every push to `main`.
- `deploy.yml` is unchanged: staging and production deploy after every successful `main` run, and the staging canary sweep still runs every time.
- `pnpm test scripts/ci/select.test.ts` fails if a path rule changes without being meant.
- The re-measurement in step 6 is posted here.

## Not in this issue

- **Gating the Deploy workflow by changed paths.** A `workflow_run` payload does not say how many commits a push carried, so the tip's diff can miss a Submission-path change earlier in the same push, and a privacy invariant is a release blocker (SPEC §7). Revisit only with a reliable push range, for example by diffing against the last deployed SHA.
- **`cancel-in-progress: true` on the preview group.** It interrupts a half-applied Alchemy deploy or destroy; the revision guard removes the same waste without interrupting anything.
- **Workflow-level `paths:` filters.** A filtered run reports no check at all, so a reviewer cannot tell "not needed" from "not reported".
- **Caching Playwright browsers in the `e2e` job.** Worth about 30 s per run; measure it before adding a cache key.
- **Splitting the `check` job.** The suite is the dominant step (62 s) and runs in parallel with nothing today; splitting would buy ~25 s of wall time and pay a second setup.

## Status

Steps 1–5 are drafted in a working tree and still need review, commit and one pull request. The pull request itself exercises the new path: it touches `scripts/ci` and `preview.yml`, so it gets a stage, an end-to-end run and a privacy read-back, and skips the canary sweep and the Lighthouse gate.

content.content:
## 7. Quality requirements

- **Privacy tests are release blockers.** The suite proves at least the following. An anonymous submission has no stored path back to a person. Every result view respects the minimum group size, including subtraction across groups. Logs from the submission path contain no identifiers. Exports and the MCP server obey the same rules.
- **Performance.** The answer page reaches first paint (the screen with the anonymity statement) in under 1 second and shows the first Question's text in under 1.3 seconds, measured as the 75th percentile on a mid-range phone. The text needs one round trip, because the Invitation token is only in the URL fragment (ADR 0005, ADR 0008). Answer submission completes in under 300 ms at the 95th percentile. The results page renders in under 1.5 seconds for a team with two years of weekly rounds.
- **Reliability.** No invitation is sent twice. No invitation is skipped silently. Failed sends show up in the lead's view with the reason.
- **Accessibility.** WCAG 2.2 AA on every page. The answer flow works with a screen reader and with a keyboard alone.
- **Testing approach.** Test behavior through the domain services and the API, not internal functions. Swap Effect layers for in-memory adapters in unit tests. Run a small set of end-to-end tests against a real preview stage, covering create pulse, receive invitation, answer from email, close round, see results, and create action.

## 8. Release plan

Each release is usable on its own. Ship a release to a real team (your own, first) before starting the next.

**Release 1. The core loop for one team.**
Sign-in with an email code, plus organization and team setup by hand. Pulses from templates, with rating, choice, and text questions. Weekly cadence with time zones. Email invitations with one-tap first answers, and reminders. Anonymous mode with the minimum group size. Round results with trends and sample sizes. Actions with owner and status, shown in the next invitation. The full privacy test suite. Preview environments per pull request.

**Release 2. Insight.**
Comment redaction and themes. Discussion guide. Team health overview with action markers. Delayed sharing. The member's private history page. German translation, deferred: English only for now (ADR 0025).

**Release 3. Organizations.**
Enterprise SSO and Directory Sync. Nested teams and leadership roll-ups with subtraction-safe thresholds. Standard questions and cross-team comparison. Confidential mode. Audit log. Exports.

**Release 4. Where people already work.**
Slack app. Microsoft Teams app. Question rotation. Action follow-up questions.

**Release 5. Open up.**
Public API, webhooks, and the MCP server. "Ask your results". Issue tracker sync for actions.

## 9. Out of scope

- Individual performance reviews, 360 reviews, and anything that scores a single person. Those features change what members believe the tool is for, and they would erode trust in anonymous team health data.
- A general-purpose form builder. SurveyBeat asks short, recurring questions. Leads who need branching logic, file uploads, or 40-question forms should use a form tool.
- Industry benchmarks against other companies' data. Revisit this only when there is enough data and a legal basis to pool it.
- Native mobile apps. Email, chat, and a fast mobile web page cover the need.

## 10. Open questions for the product owner

These need a decision from the product owner. Each one has a default you can build against until someone answers.

1. Should members see raw comments, or only themes? Default is themes only, with the lead able to show raw comments if the minimum group size is met.
2. What is the default minimum group size? Default is 4, with 3 as the floor.
3. Is self-serve sign-up for small teams wanted, or is the product sold to organizations only? Default is self-serve, with an organization created at first sign-in.
4. Which AI models are acceptable for comment processing, given data residency? Default is Workers AI models only, through AI Gateway with logging of prompts turned off.
5. What is the target market's main chat tool, Slack or Microsoft Teams? This decides which one ships first in release 4. Default is Slack.
6. Is the "surveybeat.com" domain still owned and pointed at Cloudflare? The old Terraform config assumed so.
=====
Found on production 2026-11-18. The "Claude Test" Round opened at 06:00 Berlin (alarm ran at 05:00:00 UTC, outcome ok) and no Invitation email arrived.

## Evidence (production)
- Round `ac73853b…`: `status: open`, `openedAt` 05:00:00.417 UTC, but `plannedOpenDate: 2026-11-24` and `plannedCloseAt` Nov 25 05:00 UTC although `answerWindowDays: 1`.
- D1 `invitation_index` is empty for every Round; `email_message` holds only click-driven emails (test sends, "added to Team").
- Main Worker logs: no queue activity after the 05:00 alarm.

## Bug 1: changing a Pulse's cadence moves the instant but not the date
`updateScheduledRoundForPulse` updated `planned_open_at`/`planned_close_at` but not `planned_open_date`. `executeOpenJob` recomputes send times from `plannedOpenDate`, so the Round opened on the new day and scheduled every Invitation a week later (on the stale date). It also ignored skipped weeks, unlike `scheduleNextRound`.

## Bug 2: sends created inside the Organization Durable Object are never queued
Only Worker HTTP handlers (`EmailOutbox`, `queueEmail`) write to the `Email` queue; the Organization object has no queue binding. Every send it creates on its own stays `Pending` forever: Round-open Invitations, scheduled `send` jobs, reminders, results-ready emails, and Resend Invitation.

## Fix
- One pure `nextRoundSlot` (date + instants, skipped weeks) used by both scheduling paths; the update writes the date too.
- Transactional outbox in the Organization object: a send it creates or requeues writes an `email_outbox` row in the same transaction and pulls the alarm to now; the alarm `sendBatch`es the rows through a `WriteQueue` bound in the object's init phase and deletes exactly the rows it sent. Delivery claims each send once, so a repeated message is harmless.
C:
Verified on production after #240 deployed (2026-11-18):
- Cancelled the stuck Round `ac73853b…` and moved the "Claude Test" Pulse to Wednesday 08:30 Berlin. The scheduled Round moved to `plannedOpenDate: 2026-11-18`, opening 07:30 UTC and closing 2026-11-19 07:30 UTC, so the date and instants agree.
- The Round opened at 07:30 UTC. Both Invitations reached the inbox at 07:30:07 and 07:30:09 UTC (the inbox and its `+member` address).
- `POST submit.surveybeat.app/exchange` with the real Round token returned 200 with the Pulse's 6 Questions. A real Round Invitation now works on the answer path, not only a test one.
====
## Why
Members must get a Round's Invitation by email at the time the Pulse says. On 2026-11-18 the "Claude Test" Round opened on production at 06:00 Berlin (alarm ran, outcome ok) and nobody got an email: D1 `invitation_index` is empty for every Round, and the Round's `plannedOpenDate` was 2026-11-24 although it opened on the 18th. Fixes #238.

## What changed
- **Round date (bug 1).** `updateScheduledRoundForPulse` updated the open instant but not `planned_open_date`; `executeOpenJob` recomputes send times from the date, so Invitations went on a `send` job a week later. A pure `nextRoundSlot` (domain `Lifecycle.ts`) now gives date and instants to both `scheduleNextRound` and the update, which writes the date too. It avoids skipped weeks and every date another Round of the Pulse holds, since `round` is unique on `(pulse_id, planned_open_date)` including cancelled Rounds.
- **Outbox (bug 2).** Only Worker HTTP handlers wrote to the Email queue, so every send the Organization object created itself stayed `Pending`. `organization/EmailOutbox.ts` wraps the object's SendStore: a Pending create or a requeue inserts an `email_outbox` row in the same transaction and calls `repairAlarm`, which now targets `min(now, next job)` while rows wait. The alarm runs due jobs, sends up to 100 rows per batch through `Cloudflare.Queues.WriteQueue` (bound in the object's init phase, `WriteQueueBinding` provided on `OrganizationLive`), then deletes `id <= last sent`. A crash between send and delete repeats a message; `deliver` claims each send once.
- Worker-created sends now get a second queue message (Worker EmailOutbox plus the object's outbox). Harmless; removing the Worker side is #239.

## Verification
- `nextRoundSlot` property test (weekday, open instant ahead, instants recomputed from the date, first free date) fails on two planted bugs.
- New adapter test on local workerd moves a Pulse's cadence, runs the open job, and waits for the Invitation in `captured_email`. It fails with the outbox dispatch removed (no email) and with the old date SQL (`expected 1794988800000 to equal 1795420800000`).
- Full gate locally: typecheck, ledger, comments, format, lint, 1203 unit and 241 privacy tests. Organization.test.ts passed 4 runs in a row.
- Fixture changes: the Round lifecycle route waits for the alarm to return to the earliest job once the outbox drains; the test-Invitation route uses a per-run admin address; the Submission exchange test retries a 5xx, because local D1 throws a transient "Failed to get session commit token" under the extra consumer writes.

## Not covered
- If the Email queue is down longer than the platform's alarm retries, waiting rows sit until the next send, job, or the daily cron `repairAlarm`.
- The production Round opened today still has its Invitations on a job for 2026-11-24; this change does not rewrite it.

- `POST submit.surveybeat.app/exchange` with the real Round token returned 200 with the Pulse's 6 Questions. A real Round Invitation now works on the answer path, not only a test one.
====
## Why
Members must get a Round's Invitation by email at the time the Pulse says. On 2026-11-18 the "Claude Test" Round opened on production at 06:00 Berlin (alarm ran, outcome ok) and nobody got an email: D1 `invitation_index` is empty for every Round, and the Round's `plannedOpenDate` was 2026-11-24 although it opened on the 18th. Fixes #238.

## What changed
- **Round date (bug 1).** `updateScheduledRoundForPulse` updated the open instant but not `planned_open_date`; `executeOpenJob` recomputes send times from the date, so Invitations went on a `send` job a week later. A pure `nextRoundSlot` (domain `Lifecycle.ts`) now gives date and instants to both `scheduleNextRound` and the update, which writes the date too. It avoids skipped weeks and every date another Round of the Pulse holds, since `round` is unique on `(pulse_id, planned_open_date)` including cancelled Rounds.
- **Outbox (bug 2).** Only Worker HTTP handlers wrote to the Email queue, so every send the Organization object created itself stayed `Pending`. `organization/EmailOutbox.ts` wraps the object's SendStore: a Pending create or a requeue inserts an `email_outbox` row in the same transaction and calls `repairAlarm`, which now targets `min(now, next job)` while rows wait. The alarm runs due jobs, sends up to 100 rows per batch through `Cloudflare.Queues.WriteQueue` (bound in the object's init phase, `WriteQueueBinding` provided on `OrganizationLive`), then deletes `id <= last sent`. A crash between send and delete repeats a message; `deliver` claims each send once.
- Worker-created sends now get a second queue message (Worker EmailOutbox plus the object's outbox). Harmless; removing the Worker side is #239.

## Verification
- `nextRoundSlot` property test (weekday, open instant ahead, instants recomputed from the date, first free date) fails on two planted bugs.
- New adapter test on local workerd moves a Pulse's cadence, runs the open job, and waits for the Invitation in `captured_email`. It fails with the outbox dispatch removed (no email) and with the old date SQL (`expected 1794988800000 to equal 1795420800000`).
- Full gate locally: typecheck, ledger, comments, format, lint, 1203 unit and 241 privacy tests. Organization.test.ts passed 4 runs in a row.
- Fixture changes: the Round lifecycle route waits for the alarm to return to the earliest job once the outbox drains; the test-Invitation route uses a per-run admin address; the Submission exchange test retries a 5xx, because local D1 throws a transient "Failed to get session commit token" under the extra consumer writes.

## Not covered
- If the Email queue is down longer than the platform's alarm retries, waiting rows sit until the next send, job, or the daily cron `repairAlarm`.
- The production Round opened today still has its Invitations on a job for 2026-11-24; this change does not rewrite it.

# English is the only shipped language for now; German stays a path back

English is the only language the app, the answer page, the landing page, and emails ship in. This supersedes the Release 2 German rollout of [ADR 0018](0018-german-localization.md) for now, and the German landing page in [ADR 0020](0020-landing-page-is-a-static-site-worker.md).

- **Shipped language:** `Locale` is `Schema.Literals(["en"])`. The `Locale` type, `messagesFor(locale)`, the `Record<Locale, …>` tables, and the API fields `locale`, `detectedLocale`, and `defaultLocale` stay, so a language comes back by adding its literal.
- **Removed:** the German catalogs, the German answer page (`/de/a`), the German landing page (`/de/`), the German weekly team health Template, the account menu's language field, and the Settings "Default language" section.
- **Kept:** the typed-catalog approach, so a missing key, an extra key, or a wrong `{placeholder}` still fails typecheck. Redaction's German phone-number cases stay.
- **Stored values:** rows that already hold `de` read back as unset (`person.locale`, `person.detected_locale`) or as English (`organization.default_locale`, the locale of a stored email). No migration rewrites them.
- **Bringing German back:** add the literal to `Locale`, a catalog per surface (web, answer, emails), the bilingual weekly team health Template, an answer page per locale with its own budget check, and the language picker. The stored values then read as German again without a migration.

## Consequences

- Every page and email renders in English. A `lang=de` or `/de/` link falls back to English.
- A Person who had chosen German no longer sees the German UI, and cannot change the language in the app. The API still accepts a language, so a later client can set one.
- Adding a language is a code change in the catalogs and the Template, not a data migration.

# Next round of GitHub issues: proposed plan

## Where things stand (2026-11-18)

- The core loop works on production up to the answer. #240 fixed the Invitation bug (#238), and a real "Claude Test" Round opened at 07:30 UTC today. Both Invitations arrived, and `/exchange` answered 200. The Round closes **2026-11-19 07:30 UTC**.
- Nothing after "answer" has run on production yet: reminders, close, Results, Actions, and Actions showing up in the next Invitation.
- **Results will be blank for this Round.** The "Claude Test" Team has 2 People, and the minimum group size is 4 (floor 3, `packages/domain/src/Policy.ts:24`). Close and Results are verified in Wave 1 on the 3–4-Person Team #94 calls for.
- The SPEC §7 end-to-end flow (`infra/tests/e2e/flow.spec.ts`) is still all `test.fixme`. That is why #238 reached production: nothing tested "Round opens → email arrives" across Workers.
- German was removed (ADR 0025), so #151 and the German parts of #137 and #232 are obsolete.

## Proposed issues

**Wave 1: finish Release 1 on production** (SPEC §8 says to ship to a real Team before the next release)

1. **Watch the first Round through close (update #94).** Watch tomorrow's close, the reminder and the Results-ready email. Then open a Round on a Team of 3–4 People with the group size set to 3, so Results, an Action, and that Action in the next Invitation are actually seen. Also do the Gmail, Outlook and iCloud seed test, which needs your inboxes.
2. **New: SPEC §7 flow end-to-end on a real stage.** Deploy the `SubmissionWorker` in the e2e stack, or run `flow.spec.ts` against the PR preview stage. Then replace the 7 `fixme` steps with steps that read `captured_email`. This is the regression net #238 lacked. It's the largest item.
3. **New, split from #232: "Who was invited, who was not and why."** SPEC §7 says no Invitation may be skipped silently. A Round with nobody to invite, or a Member added after the Round opened, currently shows nothing. **You need to decide where this shows:** the Rounds row, the Team checklist, or Failed emails.
4. **New, split from #232: Results, history and overview titles use the window's open date.** #235 fixed the Rounds list. `results.ts:733`, `history.ts:149` and `overview.ts` still use `plannedOpenDate`. Small; I'd do it directly.

**Wave 2: cleanup that is already scoped**

5. **#239: remove the Worker-side `EmailOutbox`.** Include the test-route race noted in its comment. This should come before #2, so the e2e flow tests a single dispatcher.
6. **#230: CI preview gating.** Steps 1–5 are drafted in a working tree. They need review, a PR, and the measurement a week later.
7. **#232 leftover: `/auth/session` answers 401 when signed out.** I propose closing this as "leave it". Changing it changes the API contract to remove a console line.

**Wave 3: polish map #137**

8. **Signed-in visual pass on staging.** Screenshot every screen at desktop and 393 px, light and dark, and file the findings as small issues. Update #137's destination to English only.

**Close or shrink**

- **Close #151** (German wording review). ADR 0025 made it obsolete.
- **#216** (lint restyle): keep it as an ongoing background item, rule by rule. It doesn't block anything.

## Suggested order

#4 and #239 now, in parallel. #94's watch starts tomorrow at close. #3 once you've chosen where it shows. #2 after #239. #230 whenever you like. #137's visual pass last.

Part of #137. Regression net for the class of bug in #238.

## Why
SPEC §7 asks for end-to-end tests against a real stage covering create Pulse, receive Invitation, answer from email, close Round, see Results, create Action. `infra/tests/e2e/flow.spec.ts` holds all seven steps as `test.fixme`, because the local e2e stack (`infra/tests/e2e/stack.ts`) deploys only the `MainWorker`, not the `SubmissionWorker`. #238 reached production because nothing tested "the Organization object opens a Round → an Invitation email exists".

## Scope
- Make the answer step reachable: either deploy the `SubmissionWorker` in the e2e stack (bound to the Main Worker's Organization namespace, as #234 does in `infra/alchemy.run.ts`), or run `flow.spec.ts` only against the PR preview stage via `E2E_BASE_URL`. Pick one and record why in the PR.

- Use enough People to clear the minimum group size (`Policy.groupSize.minimum` is 3), so "see the Results" shows a score, not the below-threshold state.

Base directory for this skill: /home/ubuntu/.claude/skills/gitbutler

# GitButler CLI Skill

Use GitButler CLI (`but`) as the default version-control interface.

## Start Here

Choose the narrowest first command by task; avoid ritual status checks:

```bash
# Selected dirty files/hunks:
but diff

# Commit order, branch/stack placement, conflict overview:
but status

# File IDs, per-commit files, amend details:
but status -fv

# What one applied branch or commit changed, for review:
but diff <branch-or-commit>

# Details for one known branch or commit:
but show <id>
```

Do not run plain `but status` and then `but status -fv` unless the compact output lacks file details needed for the task.

For "commit just/only/specific changes on a new branch", use the fast path:

```bash
but diff
but commit -b <branch> -m "<msg>" <id> <id>
```

`but commit -b <branch> ...` creates the branch when it does not exist and prints the created commit. Do not run a separate `but branch new`, status command, or verification diff unless the task needs workspace information that the result does not provide.

In a linked worktree, such as `.claude/worktrees/*`, omit `-b` so the commit goes on the branch the worktree has checked out. Use that branch as the new branch; do not stack another one on it.

## IDs

The first token on each `but diff` / `but status` line is that line's ID. When a command needs an ID, copy it exactly from the current output; never hardcode or invent one. ID lifetimes differ by entity:

- Changes and sources are **positional, space-separated** IDs (`but commit -b feat -m "msg" uvw:2e4 uvw:e2c`). An uncommitted hunk ID is written `<file-id>:<hunk-id>` (e.g. `uvw:2e4`, copied from bare `but diff`) — the part after the colon is the hunk's ID, **not** a line range (`uvw:16-40` is invalid). Do not invent flags like `--changes` / `--hunk` / `--ids`, pass a line range, or comma-separate IDs — `uvw,qyo` is parsed as one ID and fails.
- `but diff` is the exception: it accepts at most **one** target. Bare `but diff` shows all uncommitted files; inspect committed files or other entities one target at a time — never `but diff <id> <id>`.
- A committed file is `<commit-id>:<file-id>` (e.g. `mzm:uvw`, shown under each commit). A committed hunk is `<commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id>` and is shown by `but diff <commit-id>`. `@` means the uncommitted area.
- Commit IDs are stable change IDs that survive history edits (`amend`, `squash`, `move`, `uncommit`, `reword`). Commits without a change ID (e.g. upstream-only) lead with a sha prefix instead, and `#N`-suffixed refs disambiguate duplicates — both go stale after history edits, and a stale sha can silently resolve to the wrong commit. The `(sha …)` on verbose commit lines is informational — do not pass it to commands.
- Branch short IDs are snapshot-local selectors. Use full branch names for branch-targeting mutations; short IDs are safe only for immediate read-only inspection.
- File/hunk IDs copied from one diff read generally remain usable across chained commits. If one stops resolving, re-read `but diff` and retry.

**Chaining:** mutation output is concise by default, so you may chain mutations with `&&` off one inspection read. Do not chain branch short IDs through mutations; use full branch names. Add `--status-after` only when the next step needs workspace IDs or details that the mutation result does not provide. Chained `but commit` calls stack in the order written — the first is oldest, each later one goes on top. History edits may run in sequence when every commit ref involved is a change-ID ref; run them one at a time with `--status-after` when a ref is sha-based or `#N`-suffixed, or when the next command needs freshly issued IDs. Chaining `but uncommit <id> && but diff` is safe because bare `diff` needs no ID from the uncommit output. Never pipe a mutation through `tail` or `head`: the pipeline then exits with their status, so the next `&&` runs even when the mutation failed.

## Non-Negotiable Rules

1. Use `but` for all write operations. Never run `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`, `git fetch`, `git pull`, `git checkout`, `git merge`, `git rebase`, `git stash`, or `git cherry-pick`; `but pull --check` fetches. The only exceptions are selecting a side of a conflicted submodule in resolution mode (see Resolve conflicted commits) and creating a missing target branch (see Notes). If the user says a `git` write command, translate it to `but` and run that.
2. Mutation commands print their result without appending workspace status. Add `--status-after` only when the next step needs resulting workspace IDs or details; otherwise trust the mutation result and do not run a verification status/diff.
3. Branches marked `(merged upstream)` have landed; start new work on another branch. That marker alone does not mean `but pull` removes them: run `but pull --check` first. `but pull` removes only branches listed `[integrated]` ("has been integrated upstream and removed locally", or "has been merged into <target> and removed" when the target has no upstream) and rebases the rest, which stay applied. To clear a landed branch that stays applied, use `but unapply <branch>` (acts on its whole stack) rather than `but discard`. `push` and mutations (`commit`, `amend`, `squash`, `uncommit`, `reword`, `move`) refuse landed branches and commits, `absorb` skips them with a notice, and `commit` skips them when picking a default target.
4. Keep going between routine `but` commands. Put any status note in the same message as the next command, and don't end a turn on a summary that announces the next `but` step without running it. Finish with a concise summary.
5. Prefer this skill and `but skill reference` over exploratory help calls. Use `<command> --help` when required syntax is missing or a command fails; use top-level help only when you genuinely need to discover an undocumented command.
6. Other agents may share this checkout, so `@` can hold their edits. Commit, amend, and discard only the IDs or paths you changed. Bare `but commit`, `but absorb`, `but discard @`, and `git stash` take their work too, and a refusal naming files you didn't edit means you selected theirs.

## Command Patterns

- Initialize a Git repository: `but init` (current directory) or `but -C <path> init`. Non-interactive; creates no commits, remotes, or GitButler workspace. Existing repositories are left unchanged. In a repository with no commits, make the first commit with a bare `but commit -m "<msg>"`; `-b` is refused there.

- Commit: `but commit -b <branch> -m "<msg>" <id> <id>` — `-b <branch>` creates the branch if it does not exist
- Commit everything uncommitted: `but commit -b <branch> -m "<msg>"` (omit the IDs)
- Several commits from one diff: chain `but commit` calls with `&&` (commits stack oldest-first)
- Never pass `-s` to `commit`, `move`, or `pick`: it is `--switch`, not git's `--signoff`, and it unapplies every other stack.
- The branch is never positional (`but commit <branch>` fails; use `-b`), `but amend` always needs `-t`, and `but diff` takes one target (use a shared `dir/` or one call each).
- Commit at a specific history position: `--above <commit-or-branch>` or `--below <commit-or-branch>` (mutually exclusive). With a branch target, add `-b <new-name>` to name the new branch; otherwise its name is generated. The name must not already exist. Do not combine `-b` (even without a name) with commit/worktree targets.
- Targeting is **required** when more than one **stack** is applied; without it `but commit` fails with "Unclear where to commit. Found more than one stack". Several branches stacked together count as one stack — an untargeted commit then silently lands on the stack's top branch, so pass `-b` whenever the branch matters.
- Always pass `-m "<msg>"` (or `-F -` with a heredoc, `-F <file>` with a file outside the repository, or `--no-message`) to `but commit`, and to `but squash` whenever its sources are commits or branches unless the target is `@` (squash also takes `-u` to keep the target's message) — those compose a new message; without a flag an agent run keeps whatever the command composed (empty for `but commit`, the joined source messages for `but squash`) and a terminal opens an editor. Squash sources that are uncommitted or committed changes reuse the target's message and need no flag; squashing into `@` rejects message flags outright.
- Amend: `but amend -t <commit-or-branch> <file-or-hunk-id> <file-or-hunk-id>` — a branch target resolves to its newest commit
- Uncommit: `but uncommit <commit-id>` (whole commit), `but uncommit <branch>` (all commits and remove branch), `but uncommit <commit-id>:<file-id>` (committed file), or `but uncommit <commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id>` (committed hunk); committed files and hunks may be mixed, but all must come from one commit
- Copy commits (sources stay unchanged): `but pick <sha> [<sha>...] -b <new-branch>` puts the copies on a new independent branch from the target, `-b <existing-branch>` on that applied branch's tip, and `--above <branch> -b <new-name>` (or `--below`) on a new branch stacked there. Pick applies sources in the order given, so pass them oldest first. For a branch that is not applied, list SHAs with `git log --reverse <target>..<branch>` and inspect them with `git show` or `but show <sha>`; `but diff` and the IDs that `but branch show` prints for it do not work.
- Move committed changes into an existing commit or `@`: `but squash <commit-id>:<file-id> -t <commit-id-or-@>` for a committed file; `but squash <commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id> -t <commit-id-or-@>` for a committed hunk; all sources must come from one commit
- Move committed changes into a new commit at a chosen position: `but move <commit-id>:<file-id> --above <commit-or-branch> -m "<msg>"` for a committed file; `but move <commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id> --above <commit-or-branch> -m "<msg>"` for a committed hunk (`--below`, `--branch`, and `--unstack` also work)
- `but split` and a `but move` of committed changes name their new commit with `-m` or `-F` too; without either the commit gets an empty message. `but move` rejects `-m`/`-F` for whole-commit and branch sources.
- Move commit to branch top: `but move <commit-id> -b <branch>`
- Move commits or committed changes onto a new named branch: `but move <source> --above <branch> -b <new-name>` (`--below` also works); use `but move <source> --unstack -b <new-name>` for an independent branch. Omit `-b` for a generated name. Naming is not supported when stacking or unstacking a branch source.
- Discard: `but discard <id> [<id>...]` — accepts branches, commits, committed changes, uncommitted changes, or `@` for all uncommitted changes
- Push: `but push <top-branch>` — pushes the selected branch and its ancestors; to update a stack, select its top branch once and never loop. Bare `but push` pushes all unpushed work when run non-interactively — one push per stack (its topmost unpushed branch, ancestors included), and the output lists every branch it pushed. It exits non-zero if any stack failed; stacks that already pushed stay pushed, and rerunning after fixing the failure is safe (up-to-date stacks are skipped). `but push` and `but pr new` replace the remote branch: if others may have pushed to it, bring their commits in first (see Bring in commits pushed to a branch's own remote).
- Create PR: `but pr new <branch-name> [-m "Title..."] [-F - | -F <file>] [-t] [--draft]` — auto-pushes first; do not run `but push` before it

## Task Recipes

### Update workspace from main

For "get latest from main", "update/sync this workspace", "rebase onto main", or "pull main":

1. `but pull` — one command; no preflight needed. Its output reports the resulting state, and `but undo` reverts it. Uncommitted changes that conflict with the update get conflict markers and show as `{conflicted}`; resolve them as in Conflicts in uncommitted files.
2. If commits come back conflicted, resolve them with the `but resolve conflicts <branch>` and `but resolve apply` loop in Resolve conflicted commits, one branch at a time. When `HEAD` is `gitbutler/workspace`, `but pull` prints `but resolve <commit>` as the next step; that is edit mode, which is only for running code against a resolution.

`but pull --check` answers "would this conflict?" without updating. Do not use it as a routine
preflight; use it when the user asks for a preview, you need a fetch, repository policy requires one, other agents'
branches may move, or an applied branch was just merged upstream (see rule 3).

Rebasing applied branches onto the latest target IS `but pull` — never `move`, `config target`, `unapply`, or raw `git pull`/`git rebase`. The base shown in status is the last FETCHED state: when `git log` shows the remote target (for example `origin/main`) ahead of it, that is exactly the update `but pull` fetches and applies — the target setting is not stale and repointing it is never the fix. Pull carries uncommitted changes along; there is no stash, so do not hand-revert files.

### Bring in commits pushed to a branch's own remote

`but pull` only rebases onto the target. Commits someone pushed to your branch's remote show in `but status` under `(upstream: on <remote>/<branch>)`, above the branch's own commits; if status may be stale, run `but pull --check` to fetch.

1. `but branch update <branch>`, once, on the branch they pushed to.
2. Then `but pull` if the target moved too. Update before pulling. If the branch was rebased since its last push (for example by an earlier `but pull`), the update leaves an empty `(no changes)` copy of a shared commit. On a single branch, `but discard` that copy by its `#N` ref. In a stack, `but undo` the update and tell the user, because the update can also move commits into the lower branch. Do not update a second time, even if `(upstream: …)` still lists commits, because a second update duplicates commits.

### Commit selected files or hunks

1. `but diff` — shows file and hunk IDs for uncommitted changes. Do not run plain `but status` first.
2. Use file IDs when whole files belong in the commit; use hunk IDs (`<file-id>:<hunk-id>`) when only part of a file belongs. Omit IDs you don't want committed. For whole files, repo-root paths or a `dir/` prefix work too (`but commit -b feat -m "msg" src/ui/ README.md`; no `./` or globs), so don't build ID lists by piping `but diff` through grep.
3. `but commit -b <branch> -m "<msg>" <id1> <id2>` — the branch is created if it does not exist, so no prior `but branch new` is needed.
4. When the task requires knowing which changes remain, add `--status-after`; otherwise the created-commit result is sufficient.

Edge case: if wanted and unwanted edits are in the same diff hunk, GitButler cannot split that hunk by ID. Only when the task requires keeping part of that hunk uncommitted, temporarily edit the working tree to isolate the wanted lines, commit those IDs, then restore the leftover lines so they remain uncommitted.

### Amend into existing commit

1. `but status -fv` for the target commit ID and file IDs; `but diff` for hunk IDs when only part of a file belongs.
2. `but amend -t <commit-id> <id> <id>` — one command per target commit. For several target commits, chain the amends with `&&` when every target is a change-ID ref; otherwise run them one at a time with `--status-after` to get fresh refs.

### Split an existing commit

For a two-way split, move selected committed files or hunks directly into a new commit:

1. `but diff <source-commit-id>` — read committed file and hunk IDs.
2. `but split <committed-file-or-hunk-id> [<committed-file-or-hunk-id>...] -m "<message>"` — sources may mix files and hunks, but must come from one commit. The command creates the named commit immediately above the source and leaves unselected changes and the original message in the source. No follow-up reword is needed for the new commit.
3. Add `--status-after` only when the next step needs workspace IDs or details not provided by the mutation result.

For more than two replacement commits, repeat `but split ... -m "<message>"` using the remaining source's committed changes, or use the uncommit/recommit workflow below when rebuilding the entire commit:

1. `but status -fv` when you need the source commit, branch name, or placement anchor.
2. `but uncommit <source-commit-id> && but diff` in one shell call exposes the commit's changes and prints the resulting file and hunk IDs.
3. Pick replacement contents from that dirty diff, not from the old committed diff.
4. Determine the requested chronological order from the user's wording, then create the replacement commits oldest-first by chaining `but commit` calls. Do not reverse that order to match `but status`, which displays commits newest-first. `-b <branch>` puts each new commit at the TOP of that branch — if the split commit had commits above it, the replacements now sit above those preserved commits.
5. **If commits from that branch must stay ABOVE the replacements, put the preserved block back on top instead of fighting anchors.** Do not anchor with `--above <top>`/`--below <top>` (sha/`#N` anchors go stale as each insert rewrites history). Move the block together so its internal order stays intact: append `&& but move <preserved-id> [<preserved-id>...] -b <branch>` to the commit chain. Change-ID refs from step 1 stay valid; wait for fresh output first if any preserved ref is sha-based or `#N`-suffixed.
6. Leave unwanted changes uncommitted. Replacements created oldest-first appear newest-first in status — that is correct; do not reorder them. Add `--status-after` to the final mutation when you need to inspect the resulting order.

### Reorder commits

`but status` displays commits newest/top first, while task specs often list history oldest to newest — translate before moving.

1. `but status` once to get commit IDs (use `-fv` only if you also need file details).
2. `but move <source> --below <target-commit>` places source immediately below target in `but status` (older in oldest-to-newest history). `--above` places it immediately above (newer). `but move <source> -b <branch>` moves it to branch top/newest.
3. For an adjacent block, run ONE move, anchored either way: `but move <block-id> <block-id> --below <following-commit-id>` or `but move <block-id> <block-id> --above <preceding-commit-id>`. Pick an anchor outside the block; source order does not matter and the block keeps its internal order. Add `--status-after` when you need to inspect the resulting order; do not move the anchor or block members again.
4. For other reorders, make the smallest set of moves.

### Squash commits

1. `but status` for commit IDs and order.
2. Name the sources positionally and the result/target commit with `-t`: `but squash <source> [<source>...] -t <target> -m "<new message>"`.
3. To collapse an entire branch into one commit, pass just the branch and no `-t`: `but squash <branch> -m "<new message>"`.
4. Multiple independent groups may run in sequence off one status read (targets keep their change-ID refs); prefer newer/top groups first. Take fresh refs only when a ref is sha-based or `#N`-suffixed.
5. Add `--status-after` to the final squash when you need to inspect the resulting history; do not re-verify with a separate status.

### Stack existing branches

To make one existing branch depend on another: `but move <child-branch-name> --above <parent-branch-name>` (use full branch names; commit reordering uses commit IDs). To unstack: `but move <branch-name> --unstack`.

**DO NOT** stack via `uncommit` + `branch delete` + `branch new --above`, and do not use `but undo` to unstack.

### Work in a linked worktree

Use a worktree when the task needs a separate checkout, for example to build or test one branch while other work stays in the main checkout.

1. `but worktree new <branch-name>` checks out that branch in a new directory, creating it if needed (an existing branch must not be in the workspace), and prints that directory. Add `-A <commit>` to start the branch at that commit instead of the workspace base. Worktrees made by other tools must sit outside the repository directory or be listed in `.git/info/exclude`; otherwise a bare `but commit` in the main checkout records them in the branch.
2. Run `but` from that directory, or with `but -C <path>`. There, a bare `but commit -m "<msg>"` or `but diff` takes that worktree's changes, a bare path names a file there, and the commit goes on the worktree's branch. Do the work on that branch, also in a worktree another tool made. `-b <new-name>` is refused there; stack a new branch on it only when the user asks for a separate branch. If `but` says the worktree "is not managed by GitButler", it is archived: `but worktree unarchive <name>`. `but undo` refuses to restore a branch a worktree has checked out, so reverse a mistake there with the inverse command (`uncommit`, `reword`).
3. `but status` from any checkout shows the worktree as a lane of its own, with the same IDs everywhere. `@` always means the main worktree's uncommitted changes; `<worktree>:@` names a linked worktree's changes from anywhere.
4. Push and open PRs as for any branch (`but pr new <branch-name>`). `but pull` also rebases worktree branches. If that leaves a worktree commit `{conflicted}`, the branch name doesn't find it: take its commit ID from `but status` and run `but resolve conflicts <commit-id>`, then `but resolve apply <path>:<N> --commit <commit-id>`.
5. When done, `but worktree remove <name>` deletes the directory and keeps the branch. It refuses while the worktree has uncommitted changes; `-f` discards them.

### Create or manage pull requests

`but pr new <branch-name>` pushes the selected branch and its ancestors, then creates the PR in one step — no prior `but push`. Provide `-F -` with a heredoc or `-F <file>` (first line is the title), `-t`, or `-m` with real newlines (zsh/bash: `-m $'Title\n\nBody'`) so no editor opens. Do not write the message to a file inside the repository: the next `but commit` would commit it. If forge auth is missing, ask the user to run `but config forge auth` in a terminal; it refuses non-interactive runs.

If you do create a PR for a stacked branch, use `but pr` — not `gh pr create` (only `but pr` sets PR bases and stack metadata; `gh pr create` breaks that). To publish a whole stack: `but pr new <top-branch-name> -t`. Manage with `but pr auto-merge|set-draft|set-ready <selector>`; selectors can be a branch name, current branch/stack CLI ID, or numeric review ID. See `but skill reference` for details.

When `but pr new` prints a `<pr-created>` line, copy that line into the text of your reply. It tells the app running you that this session opened the PR.

### Dependency conflict with another branch

Changes that build on another branch's commits cannot land on an independent branch. `but commit` and `but amend` fail atomically ("Cannot commit: N changes could not be applied"), naming the branch and commit each rejected change depends on — nothing is committed and no `-b` branch is created.

Stack only when your change builds on that branch's code. A refusal can also mean your hunk only borders lines that branch changed (a doc line, a lockfile): then leave one unchanged line between your edit and theirs, or keep that hunk uncommitted until that branch lands, and commit the rest. Never drop or rewrite real work to get past a refusal; ask the user.

When there is a single dependency branch, the error's Hint gives the exact recovery command: `but move <your-branch> --above <dependency-branch>` to stack an existing branch on its dependency, or `but branch new <name> --above <dependency-branch>` when the target branch didn't exist yet. Run it, then retry the original command. When the error names dependencies without a Hint (several dependency branches, or the dependency is on the target branch itself), run `but status -fv` to see where the dependent commits live before choosing a placement.

If that recovery command fails, do NOT try `uncommit`, `squash`, or `undo` as a workaround — re-run `but status -fv` to confirm both branches exist and are applied, then retry with exact branch names.

### Resolve conflicted commits (after pull, move, or reorder)

**NEVER use `git add`, `git commit`, `git checkout --theirs/--ours`, or any git write command during resolution.** Only `but resolve` commands plus direct file edits. The one exception is a conflicted submodule in edit mode, below.

Conflicts do not interrupt operations in GitButler: a rebase always completes, and commits that conflicted are marked `{conflicted}` in `but status`. Find them from the warning that history-editing commands (`move`, `discard`, …) print, from the `but pull` summary, or from `but status`. Resolve them one conflict at a time, without entering any mode. Work through one branch at a time, oldest commit first — the loop is:

1. `but resolve conflicts <branch>` — shows the conflicts of that branch's oldest conflicted commit, numbered per file. Each conflict has three sections: `ours` (the new base the commit was rebased onto), `base` (common ancestor), and `theirs` (the commit's own version). Without a branch it picks the first conflicted branch and tells you which; the output also says when other conflicted commits exist.
2. Apply one resolution per command:
   - Merged/mixed content (the common case — combine the intent of both sides): pipe it to `but resolve apply <path>:<N>` via stdin (heredoc) or pass `--file <f>`. The content replaces the whole conflicted region; never include conflict markers.
   - Take a side entirely: `but resolve apply <path>:<N> --ours` or `--theirs` (bare `<path>` applies the side to all conflicts in that file).
   - Delegate one conflict to the configured AI model: `but resolve apply <path>:<N> --ai` — prefer your own merged content when you have the context.

PR title: `R1 239: the Organization object is the only Email queue producer`
PR body (use exactly, ending with the attribution line):

## Why
Since #240 the Organization object's transactional outbox puts every send it creates or requeues on the Email queue. The Worker-side `EmailOutbox` still queued the same sends, so each got two queue messages and there were two dispatchers. Fixes #239.

## What changed
- Removed the domain `EmailOutbox` service and its callers (`DirectoryFlow`, `PulseFlow`), the `QueueEmail` follow-up and the resend `queue` flag, `queueEmail`, the MainWorker outbox and its Email queue producer binding (the consumer stays), and the test fakes.
- Test fixture: `TestInvitationTestRoutes` used to claim and settle a test send by hand, which raced the outbox delivering it. A test-stage-only Organization RPC, `createFailedTestSend`, now creates and fails a test send in one transaction.
- Resend of a still-Pending send no longer re-queues: its outbox row stays until the queue accepts the batch.
- `/__test/email` POST creates the fixture Organization row first, since the outbox reads it to build the queue message.

## Verification
Fence gate: typecheck, lint, format, ledger, comments, 1207 unit tests, 241 privacy tests. Adapter tests for EmailDelivery, EmailOutbox, Organization, DirectoryApi and PulsesApi pass on local workerd.

## Not covered
The test-Invitation fixture's first burst send and bulk sends still have outbox rows (since #240) and could in principle be dispatched while the route runs. Low likelihood; not changed here.

content.text:
The new round of issues is filed, and #239 is open as https://github.com/chrisdoc/surveybeat-next/pull/246. I'm watching its checks and will squash-merge it once they pass.

**Issue changes**
- **New:** #243 (the SPEC §7 flow running end-to-end on a real stage, blocked by #239) and #244 (a Round shows who was invited, who was not, and why). Both are sub-issues of the map #137, along with #239.
- **#244 placement:** I picked the Rounds row as the default place to show it, because you hadn't chosen one. Change it on the issue if you want a different spot.
- **#245 closed:** I opened it and then closed it, because #240 already fixed the cause. Round titles drifted only because a cadence change moved the open time but not the date, and #240 now updates both together. The fix would have touched about 30 files for one cancelled Round with no Results.
- **Closed:** #232, after splitting its remaining items out (I left the signed-out `/auth/session` 401 as it is), and #151, because German was removed under ADR 0025.
- **Plan comments:** #94 has the watch list for the first real Round. It closes 2026-11-19 07:30 UTC, but this Round won't show any Results. Its Team has 2 People, below the minimum group size of 4 (or 3 if lowered), so seeing Results and an Action needs one Round on a Team of 3–4 People. #137 has the order of work.

**PR #246 (#239)**
- The Worker no longer puts emails on the Email queue. The Organization object's outbox from #240 is now the only sender, so each send gets one queue message instead of two.
- The test route that fakes a failed test email no longer races automatic delivery. It now creates and fails that send in one step through a new test-stage-only call, `createFailedTestSend`.
- One behaviour change: resending a send that is still waiting to go out no longer puts it on the queue again. It already sits in the outbox until the queue accepts it.
- Checks run: typecheck, lint, format, both ledgers, 1207 unit tests and 241 privacy tests all pass. The email-related tests that run on the local Workers runtime also pass. I read the diff and the reviewer agent reviewed it; neither found a blocking issue.
- Known leftover: in that same test route, a few other test emails can still in principle be sent while the route runs. #240 introduced this and the PR doesn't change it; it's written up in the PR.

The `.githooks/*` changes in the worktree aren't part of this work and aren't committed.

Next in the order: #94's watch of tomorrow's close, then #244, then #243.

## Why
Codecov reads 0% for most Organization Durable Object code (#246: 26 of 37 missing patch lines are in `packages/cloudflare/src/Organization.ts`). Adapter tests run it through `@alchemy.run/test` `Test.make({ dev: true })`, which deploys to a separate local workerd process. Vitest's v8 coverage only sees the Node process, so the alarm, the outbox dispatch, the RPCs and the test routes count as uncovered even when a test exercises them. The patch check fails on every PR that touches the object (#234, #240, #246), so it no longer tells us anything.

Cloudflare's Workers Vitest integration (`@cloudflare/vitest-plugin` 1.8.4, peer `vitest ^4.1.0 || ^5.0.0`, so it fits our 5.1) runs tests inside workerd with direct Durable Object stubs, `runInDurableObject`, `runDurableObjectAlarm` and `evictDurableObject` ([guide](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/examples/testing-with-durable-objects/)). Coverage there is Istanbul only; v8 is not supported ([known issues](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/testing/vitest-integration/known-issues/)).

## Conflict with ADR 0008
ADR 0008 says "`vitest-pool-workers` is not used, and there is no hand-edited wrangler config." Adopting the plugin needs a new ADR that supersedes that line. The plugin can take Miniflare options inline instead of a wrangler file, which keeps "every resource is declared in `infra/alchemy.run.ts`" intact.

## Prototype first (answer these before an ADR)
1. Can the plugin load the Alchemy-defined `Organization` class (`packages/cloudflare/src/Organization.ts`, Effect runtime, SQLite migrations from `packages/cloudflare/migrations`) with bindings given inline, without a wrangler file?

content.text:
I didn't adopt the plugin in your link yet; I filed it as a prototype issue, #247. Separately, #246 is merged, which closes #239.

**Why the Cloudflare plugin fits:** the Codecov patch check fails on every change to the Organization object (#234, #240, #246). Our object tests use `@alchemy.run/test`, which runs the object in a separate local Workers process. Coverage only measures the Node process, so it reports that code as 0% even when tests run it. The plugin in your link runs the tests inside the Workers runtime instead, so coverage would count that code.

**What stops me adopting it directly:**
- **ADR 0008 forbids it.** It says the Workers test pool "is not used, and there is no hand-edited wrangler config", so adopting it needs a new ADR. The plugin can take its settings inline rather than from a wrangler file, which keeps `infra/alchemy.run.ts` as the one place resources are declared.
- **Coverage would need a second tool.** Inside the Workers runtime the plugin only supports Istanbul coverage, not v8. Its report would have to be merged with today's v8 report into the single `coverage/lcov.info` that CI uploads.
- **Version fit is fine.** `@cloudflare/vitest-plugin` 1.8.4 supports Vitest 5, which we're on.

#247 asks four questions before any ADR:
1. Can the plugin load our `Organization` class?
2. Does `Organization.ts` then show real coverage?
3. Is a test faster or slower than today's (some take up to 240 s)?
4. Can the two coverage reports be merged into one?

If the answer is no, it ends with a Codecov config that stops measuring code it can't see, so the check means something again.

**PR #246:** check, privacy, deploy, e2e and preview-privacy all passed, and I squash-merged it. CodeRabbit's review hadn't come in yet. GitHub kept the local branch because this worktree has it checked out; the remote branch is deleted.

Next in the order: #94's watch of the first real Round's close (2026-11-19 07:30 UTC), then #244, then #243. #247 can run alongside.

content.text:
Yes, it holds too much. The issue isn't the line count itself. Two modules are still inside it, and the file already shows how to pull them out. Line numbers below are from `main` at `c8dfc669`:

| Lines | What | Size |
|---|---|---|
| 108–170 | Wiring: config, SQL, stores, outbox, `repairAlarm` | ~60 |
| 182–300 | Scheduling: `scheduleNextRound`, `updateScheduledRoundForPulse`, helpers | ~120 |
| 301–1040 | **Round job runner**: open, send, remind, close, share, compute, themes, `runDueJobs`, payload decoding | **~740** |
| 1040–1160 | Pulse RPCs and the test-send helper | ~120 |
| 1161–1453 | **`runRoundCommand`**: one 9-case switch (SkipWeek … ResendInvitation) | **~290** |
| 1454–1597 | Spread-in slices, plus ~25 small RPCs (getters, `injectComputeFailures`, `createFailedTestSend`, timezone, participation) | ~140 |

**Why it's a problem:**
- **The pattern already exists and stopped halfway.** `organization/*.ts` holds Actions, Directory, Notes, Results, RoundViews, Sends, Submissions and EmailVisibility (1,296 lines). Each is a function that takes `{ rounds, directory, sql, … }` and returns RPCs. The Round lifecycle, the largest and riskiest part, never moved.
- **Decisions are mixed into the SQL calls.** `runRoundCommand` checks "team not found", "pulse not found" and "week out of range" inline, inside a transaction. The test-send path does it the better way: a pure `decideTestSend` in the domain, and the object only applies the result. Logic written inline can only be tested through workerd. That is also why coverage reads 0% (#247).
